utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, are you ready to proceed? Did we not finish with the cross-examination yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. Miss Hollis is going to do it.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Miss Hollis? OK.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. We would call Edin Mrkalj. EDIN MRKALJ, called.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I feel we should be doing something. Is there anything anyone would like to talk about? Mr. Orie, welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps there is a matter I might mention -- I can do it later.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Sir, would you take the oath that is being given to you, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. (The witness was sworn)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Sir, would you please state your name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Edin Mrkalj.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What is your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was born on 13th June 1965 in the village of Biscani in the municipality of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you live in Biscani until you were 15 and then move to Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you move back to the village of Biscani in January of 1988?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: After you moved back to Biscani how long did you live there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After I returned there I lived there until 30th -- 31st of May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: How many people live in Biscani?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About 3,000.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you know many of the people who lived there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was the ethnic composition of that village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Muslim, 100 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: If the witness could be provided with Prosecution Exhibit 79, please? Sir, if you could take a moment to look at that map and orient yourself and then if that map could be placed on the overhead projector, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did orient myself.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Sir, if you could use the pointer and if you could for the Court point to where the village of Biscani is located on that map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The village is here, in this area. This is my village, Biscani.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: If we could have a closer view of that, please? Could you point again to Biscani?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here it is, the area of Biscani.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: How far was Biscani from the town of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the first houses are some three kilometres away from Biscani. So, my village is some three kilometres away from the first hamlet.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Of the town of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the town of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: The village of Hambarine, how close to Biscani was the village of Hambarine?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About five kilometres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Can I ask you a question about this Exhibit that we have so often looked at? I do not know whether you are able to respond to it, but the little squares that are shown there I had assumed to be actual representation of houses, but the numbers that we have been getting of people, inhabitants, suggests that they are not, that there are far more houses than appear. Do you happen to know whether that is so or not? Can we regard this map as accurately representing dwellings or merely as being representational?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, my understanding is that it is a representation. I do not know if it is intended to represent individual homes. We can certainly find that out for you, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: That would be useful, thank you. MISS HOLLIS (To the witness): If you could show us, please, on this map where Hambarine is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This area here.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: The village of Rizvanovici is where?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You see it.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Could you point to that again, please? That is how far from Biscani?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is the first village next to Biscani, so in the direction of the village of Volar. To the left is the village of Rizvanovici and to the right the village of Biscani, so there is only a street separating them.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Rakovcani that is shown on this map, how far is that from Biscani?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About three kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Is this entire area referred to in general as Brdo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this whole area is called Brdo.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: To your knowledge, what was the ethnic composition of that area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The ethnic composition was Muslim, 100 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Sir, what was your previous occupation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was a policeman in charge of security.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you train in Sarajevo at the school of internal affairs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I graduated from the school in Sarajevo, the 11th class which is 79/84, the class of 79/84.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Was the first job as a policeman at the federal SUP in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What years did you work there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From 1984, that is since I graduated until 31st December 1987.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Where was the headquarters of the federal SUP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The headquarters were in the Kneza Mihajla Street 92, and the headquarters of my command was in Sarajevska Street.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: This was in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What were your duties at the federal SUP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was in charge of the security of diplomatic missions of foreign states and vital facilities of vital interest to our former common state.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did the federal SUP have special units?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What were their jobs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those were special units for protection against sabotage and subversion activities or in case of major unrest, such as in Kosovo, for instance. When it happened in Kosovo, those units were sent there.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was the difference between the federal SUP and the SUPs at the Republic level?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Republic SUP had the jurisdiction over the territory of a Republic, for instance, of a Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, whereas the federal SUP had under its jurisdiction the entire territory of our former common state of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: During the years that you worked at the federal SUP, did you become familiar with the license plates used on the vehicles of the federal SUP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was distinctive about those plates?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The plate number of federal SUP cars began with No. 9, for instance, 900.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: You indicated that you worked with the federal SUP in Belgrade until the end of December 1987. Did you then return to Biscani and begin to work as a policeman in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: How long did you work as a policeman in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I worked there until 10th April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: To your knowledge, did any police units wear blue camouflage uniforms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What kind of police units wore such uniforms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Special federal SUP units.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: When you worked as a policeman in Prijedor, how many police stations were there in the opstina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were four.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Where were they located?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The central one was in Prijedor in Mose Pijade Street, No. 4, and then we had their departments in Omarska, Kozarac and Ljubija. Those were the departments, the divisions.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Where did you work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was in the central station in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was the ethnic composition of the Prijedor police department while you worked there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, while I was there the majority of the policemen were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What were your duties in the police department in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Traffic and security.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Were you later promoted into the criminal division?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in '91, but without any promotion.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: In 1992 while you were still working for the Prijedor police department, who was the Chief of Police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Chief of Police was Hasan Talundzic.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Sorry, the Chief of Police was Hasan Talundzic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Talundzic.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was his ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: In March 1992 do you recall getting a call from a Serbian friend who wanted to talk to you urgently?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did that friend come to talk to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: How did you know this man?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We used to work together.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Where did he work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: In what organisation or agency did he work there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The federal SUP.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What did he want to talk to you about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He wanted to talk to me about the times ahead.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What did he tell you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He told me that members of his people would occupy the town, take over the power in the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: When you say "members of his people", what people are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of the Serb people.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did he tell you anything else about what was to happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That the territory of the municipality of Prijedor would be cleansed of non-Serb population, and that was the first time I heard the word "ethnic cleansing".

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did he tell you anything about his being offered a job in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in a town.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What kind of job had he been offered?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One of the executive jobs.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: In what agency or organisation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The SUP.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did your friend ever tell you how he had received this information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, he moved among people from whom he could learn quite a lot.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What did you do with this information after you received it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I decided to talk to the Chief of the Public Security Station in Prijedor and transmit to him the information.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was his reaction to this information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: His reaction was the following: he said that was of no interest, that we were -- that he was not interested, that that was not his concern, that we were not for war and that nothing would come out of it.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: In early April 1992, did you go to Belgrade to bring your daughter back from the hospital there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Had you purchased an airline ticket so that you and your daughter could travel back to Banja Luka on a commercial plane?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, to come back from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Were you able to bring your daughter back on a commercial aircraft?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: While you were in Belgrade did you hear on television that all commercial flights to Banja Luka had been cancelled?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I heard it on the Serbian television.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Were you able to arrange a flight back on a military aircraft?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: While you were waiting for the flight, were you told that you had to wait because soldiers were expected?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was told that.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: While you were waiting for the flight did you see men in uniforms coming to the area where you were waiting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I saw them.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What were these men wearing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they were in grey olive green uniforms of the former JNA.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did they have any type of insignia or other attachments to their uniforms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some had white bands, ribbons, and some had red bands so that I could divide them into two groups.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did they have weapons and gear with them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: While you were waiting for that flight did you hear these men talking amongst themselves?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What did you hear them talk about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They mentioned some incredible things. They talked about how they would get rich quickly, about money, gold -- great time.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did they mention anything about where their destination was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some were talking about Mostar, others about Bihac.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you recognise the accents or dialect of these men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did recognise it.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the Serb dialect.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was the appearance of these men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they did not look like a normal army. They were unkempt, disheveled. They simply did not look like a real, like a true army. They were not disciplined.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: During this flight back to Banja Luka, was there equipment or supplies on this military aircraft with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, when we entered the weapons ----

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: I am sorry, when you "entered the weapons"? Would you repeat that answer, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the weapons were loaded.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: So there were boxes of weapons in the aircraft?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they loaded crates on one side, the entrance, they were already there, but when we entered this space where we came in was close with I do not know how many crates more.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: When you came back from this trip did you leave the Police Force?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, for good.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What did you tell the police department?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I said I was taking a sick leave.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: After you had taken this sick leave, do you recall attending a police meeting at the mining company building in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Was this meeting before or after the Serb takeover of Prijedor on 30th April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Who called this meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Serb Crisis Committee.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Was this meeting attended by Serb representatives and all the non-Serb active duty policemen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Do you recall the names of any of the Serb representatives at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What are the names you recall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were present Simo Drljaca, then they introduced him as a minister and they said it was Kovacevic. I did not know him before. There was Dule Jankovic there, Simo Miskovic.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Simo Drljaca, if you know, at that time what was his position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After the occupation of the town of Prijedor, he was appointed the chief of the Serb station.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: The chief of the Serb police station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Dule Jankovic, what was his position, if you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was the commander of the station. He kept his previous post.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Simo Miskovic, what was his position, if you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was the SDS President, the President of the Serb Democratic Party of the municipality of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: At this meeting what demands or requests were made of the non-Serb police officers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were requested to sign a statement of loyalty, unreserved, unconditional.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Loyalty to whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Loyalty to the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you agree to sign this loyalty declaration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: In late May of 1992 did you witness any of the attacks on Hambarine and other villages in that area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What did you see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw the shelling and I experienced the shelling of that area.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What villages did you witness being shelled?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could easily see Hambarine, Rizvanovici, part of Biscani, Rakovcani.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: During this time that you saw this shelling of these villages, did you see anything that appeared to be return fire from any of those villages?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there was no return fire.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you see any tanks involved in this operation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I saw.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: During the attack and the shelling of this area, were the villages in this area given an ultimatum to surrender weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What type of weapons were to be surrendered?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The weapons of the Territorial Defence and the Reserve Police force were to be surrendered.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: How was that ultimatum delivered?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By radio.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did the announcement say by whose authority the ultimatums were given?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Crisis Committee of the Serb municipality of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: After these ultimatums were given, do you recall being involved in contacts that were made with a man called Captain Glusac about the surrender of weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is Captain Glusac.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Who was he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was a reserve Captain of the former JNA.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: If you know, what was his ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Serb.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you and others talk with him about the surrender of weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They talked about it before me and I had the opportunity on two occasions.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was his response?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, he said when we met for a second time that if our side begins fire and if any Serb is wounded or killed, then he would be issued orders to shell the area of our villages.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did the inhabitants of Biscani obey the ultimatum and surrender weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you later learn that Biscani had, nonetheless, been destroyed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: On 31st May 1992 were you given an order to turn in your police weapons the next day at the Prijedor police station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, on May 31st 1992.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Who gave you that order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The order was conveyed to me by Reserve policeman, Duro Knezevic. He said that he was coming from the central station in Prijedor and that I was to surrender, that I was to come to the station with my personal weapons and gear.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did he indicate what would happen if you refused to obey that order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did ask that question, what would happen if I did not turn up, and he replied, "Well, you know what happened to Hambarine when policeman Aziz Aliskovic refused to surrender".

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What type of weapons did you have at this time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had official weapons, a pistol and a submachine gun.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you go to the Prijedor police station on 1st June and surrender your weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Were you interrogated at the police station on that date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: By whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was interrogated by my former fellow policemen, inspectors.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Do you recall the names of any of these people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What were the names you recall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the chair of the inspector team was Mira Jankovic and there were Gostimir Modic with her, Nenad Lakic, a person I did not know who had allegedly come from Croatia and joined the ranks of the police, and Nebojsa Tomcic.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: You indicated that these people were your colleagues. To your information, what was their ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were all of Serb descent.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Were you held at the police station overnight and then the next day, 2nd June, taken to Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: How were you transported to Omarska on 2nd June?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was taken there by a bus.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Were any other detainees taken on that bus with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was the only one on that bus.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Were there other people on the bus?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Who were these people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were members of the criminal investigation department of the Serb police station of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: If you recall the names of any of these people, could you tell us who was on the bus with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On that bus were Ranko Mijic, Zare Tejic, Nebojsa Tomcic, Nebojsa Babic, Rade Knezevic, Zika Jovic, Ranko Bucalo. I do not know if I mentioned Dragic Knezevic.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: On this trip from the Prijedor police station to the Omarska camp, did you see any corpses along the route?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Were these corpses arranged in any particular positions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: How were they arranged?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first thing I saw, I saw corpses in the shape of a cross. Then I saw corpses, from that cross, two corpses. The head of one corpse was next to another corpse and then there was an arm separated from the body nearby. Then I saw a big cross made up of corpses.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: As you approached Omarska camp, do you recall seeing a fire about 300 metres from the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember the fire.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Do you recall anything unusual or particular about the smoke from that fire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The special thing I remember is the smell that emanated from the fire as we passed it and penetrated the bus.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Later in Omarska camp did you ever smell a similar type smell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. When I was together with Sekiric Ferid, his burnt hands, his arms that were burnt, such an awful stench came, the same kind of smell.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: How long were you held at the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Until the camp was disbanded.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Do you recall what month that was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In early August.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you know any of the other detainees at Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was the ethnic group of the detainees that you knew?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Were any of the guards or camp leaders at Omarska people you had known before coming to the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Who?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had known the Commander of the camp. I knew personally one of the shift commanders.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Who was the Commander of the camp that you had known previously?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: I am sorry, I do not have a translation of that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: He said he did not say "commander" but "commandant" and he asked if it was translated well. There is only one word in English, "commander", but he is making a distinction between "commander" and "commandant".

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: To your knowledge, who was the commandant of the camp, the person that you had known before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first Commander was Kvocka Miroslav, the second was Meakic Zeljko, the third one was Drago Prcac.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: How did you know these men from before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were members of the police station in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you know a man by the name of Drago Meakic before you came to the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: How did you know him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew him because he worked as an inspector in the criminal department until 1991 when he retired and joined the Serb police station in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: To your knowledge, were Drago Meakic and Zeljko Meakic related?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was the relationship?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Drago Meakic is the uncle of Zeljko Meakic.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: You indicated that you had previously known one of the shift commanders at Omarska, who was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was Mladjo Radic, nickname "Krkan", the leader of the shift No. 3.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Mladjo Radic and Zeljko Meakic, to your knowledge, were of what ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: When you first arrived at the camp of Omarska for the first few days where were you held?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was held in the repair building.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: If you could take the pointer, please, and from your seat if you could point to the building you refer to as the repair building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This is the building.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: So you are pointing to the long red building on the model?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: How long were you held in that repair building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know exactly the total number of days, but I was there the first time in a room by the staircase at the entrance. I was there until 6th, until 6th June 1992.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: So this room by the staircase, this is on the ground floor or was this on the first floor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the ground floor.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Where were you taken to from that building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After one of a number of investigations I was taken to the pista.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: When you say "the pista" would you point to the area you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will. This area between the repair building and, as we called it, administration building. It is this area that I am pointing now.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: How long were you held on the pista?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I spent most of the time there on the pista, maybe about 40 days. I am not sure exactly.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: While you were on the pista were there concrete containers on both sides of the pista area between the repair building and the administration building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Were these containers laid so that they were touching against each other or was there space between these containers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was space between the containers, yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: While you were on the pista were you ever forced to lie on your stomach for periods of time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Depending on the situation but, yes, we were forced to lie on our stomach every day.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: While you would lie on your stomach would you ever look around to see what was happening?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: With these containers on both sides of the pista as you lay on your stomach were you able to see through the spaces between the containers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were no hindrance to viewing the area.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Were you able to see above the containers to see people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, certainly -- why not?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: If I could have Prosecution Exhibit 246, please, and have that provided to the witness?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We will continue until 1 o'clock since we started late, gentlemen, and Miss Hollis -- excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Until 1 o'clock?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Normally we would recess at 11.30, but see did not start until five minutes to 11.00 -- unless I hear to the contrary from someone.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Could that photograph be placed on the overhead projector, please? (To the witness): As you look at that photograph, those containers in the photograph, are those the containers that you were speaking of earlier, the concrete containers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, those are the containers.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: As you see the spacing in this photograph, was that the type of spacing that was between those containers when you were in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was larger spacing.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: As you look at the plants in those containers, is that about the height of the plants when you were on the pista in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were smaller plants.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: So they were taller in height?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: The people in this photograph, do you recognise either of those two people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Could you tell us who those people are and point to the person as you say the name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is Simo Drljaca. This is Nada Balaban.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: How did you know ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just one moment, please. Vokic Radovan there can be seen only a little bit, only a part of Vokic Radovan, a policeman.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Could you point to -- that is the person there. How did you know Nada Balaban?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: She was the English teacher.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: If that photo could be returned to the Registry, please? While were you at Omarska camp, were you ever in the white house there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: How long were you in the white house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I spent one night there.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What room were you kept in that night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As you enter the white house, it was on the left side, the second door to the left.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was the condition of that room while you were in it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was horrible.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a small room. There were more than 20 people there. The smell in the room itself, blood, the bad smell, the urine. The people who had been lying there for a long time, they were in a very, very bad state. One of the men had started rotting. Esad Talic, doctor, the doctor, had performed surgery on him. I will never, never forget that.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you know any of the men in that room?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I recognised one man I had known him quite well, Ferid Sekiric.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was his condition?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was in a very bad condition. He had five bullets inside his body. Serbian doctors had taken out four of those bullets but one was left in his body. So he was in a very, very bad condition.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was his ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: After you had spent some 40 days on the pista where were you taken to then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After 40 days on the pista we were taken to the repair building.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Before I ask that question, I would ask you, do you know Dule Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: When did you first meet him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I met him in 1991, early 1991.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: How did you meet him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: In what circumstance did you meet him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We had a work meeting. It was held once a month usually on the occasion of the visit by the policemen from individual stations. So we used the opportunity and we would come an hour or two earlier; we would have a chat or a drink or two before the meeting. On that occasion I met Dusko Tadic through a friend of his.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Who was that friend who introduced you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My co-worker.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What is his name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Emir Karabasic.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: When Emir Karabasic introduced Dusko Tadic to you, how did he introduce him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As a good friend of his.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: This first occasion that you were with Dusko Tadic, how long did that occasion last?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We sat together for over an hour, roughly.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: After that initial introduction did you ever see Dusko Tadic again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, several times.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Where would you see him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you ever see him any place other than Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I saw him once in Kozarac. We were in the same cafe.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: On that occasion did you have any interaction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We greeted each other, and my company paid a round of drinks for his friends and his friends paid another round for us.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Do you recall when it was that this meeting occurred?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember the date exactly.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Do you know what business or businesses Dule Tadic had?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I learnt that he had some sort of cafe, but I also knew that he was involved in karate and I had the opportunity to look in the local newspaper and read about Dusko Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: So you read about his sports activities in the paper?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He was running a karate club of sorts.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you ever go to this cafe that Dusko Tadic owned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: How many times total would you say that you saw Dule Tadic before the attacks began in opstina Prijedor in May 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could say several times, a number of times.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: During the time that you saw Dusko Tadic before the conflict, did you ever see him with a beard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you ever see him clean shaven?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I never paid any attention, much attention to that. He was with a small beard, without a beard.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Was there anything distinctive or noticeable about the way Dusko Tadic walked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he had a stagger, left to right, and he was rather puffed in the face.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: I would like to draw your attention -- you indicated he had a stagger, what do you mean by a stagger?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As he walked, he moved from side to side. He walked like an athlete, mostly to be seen, to be, you know, to stand out -- maybe an inferiority complex or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: I would like to draw your attention to 16th June 1992. On that date did you see Dusko Tadic at Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not in the camp, but I saw him in the concentration camp of Omarska. We were not camping. We were inmates of a concentration camp.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: On that date were you beaten?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was beaten.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Where did the beating take place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the first floor of the administration building at the top of the staircase.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Were you there at the top of the staircase by yourself or was there another detainee there with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was one other individual with me, I think it was a minor by the look of him. I do not know his name.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Why had the two of you been taken to the first floor of the administration building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We had been taken in order to carry out a dead body which had been killed.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What happened to you after you reached the head of the stairs on the first floor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we came to the top of the stairs we stopped. There was a traditional position, attitude, hands behind the back, face down. The first individual next to the stairs looked to me like a minor, a stranger had come with me, I had never seen him before. I was right next to him.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What happened then as you stood there at the top of the stairs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we came I heard laughter, something like laughter. I had not seen how many people there were around. At one point in time the individual next to me received a blow. I could see the rubber baton, not the entire scene because I had to look down. The stranger fell down. I saw him urinating.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When this individual came to he was told to go downstairs.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What happened to you after this younger man had been hit and fallen down?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: An individual that I had not seen before had put under my throat a rubber baton in such a way that my head was straightened up. I was no longer looking down. I could see -- I was able to see the face of the individual holding the rubber baton under my chin, roughly like this.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Who was it that you saw?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that moment I saw and recognised Dusko Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What happened after Dusko Tadic stood before you with the baton under your chin? What happened next?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All of a sudden, I did not expect a blow, he turned and I thought he was going away from me and then a horrible blow came down on me, on my head, here.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What happened after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then he asked me, "How come you are here? What brought you here?" I answered, "Voluntarily." I saw the cynicism in his face, I saw the smile, the grin, on his face. At one moment I saw next to his head at the doorway there was Rade Knezevic, the inspector.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was he doing when you say him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was standing in the doorway.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He asked me what my occupation was.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Who was it who asked you that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dusko Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What happened after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I replied that I was a policeman. He said, he told me to stretch out my arms, my hands. I did so.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: So you spread out your hands with your palms up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then he said to turn my hands the other way round. I did so. He asked me which hand I used to write. I said I was right handed.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He started hitting me on the hand with the rubber baton. I suffered the blows. Another stranger came to the place where we were and he started beating me too. At one point the rubber baton fell on the floor. Then Dusko Tadic said to me, "Pick up the baton and say, 'Here you are, sir, and Serb, Mr. Serb'." I had no choice. I knelt down, picked up the baton and as I handed him the baton I said, "Here you are, Mr. Serb". Then the barrel of the submachine gun was put into my mouth.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: By whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dusko Tadic, by Dusko Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: In what position were you when the barrel of this submachine gun was put into your mouth? Were you standing at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I was standing, but not quite straight, not quite upright, not quite normally. I had taken, perhaps it was mechanical from training, I had taken a posture somewhat lower so that I stood more firmly on my feet. There was this barrel in my mouth and then I began receiving blows on my head.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: While you received these blows on your head, was this barrel still in your mouth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That barrel was in my mouth and I was receiving double blows with a rubber baton and with the metal spring. Now, rubber baton, one can still survive, somehow manage it, but not a metal spring. My head was bursting, blood was bursting. It was awful. My teeth were breaking. Everything was breaking. I cannot remember exactly which blow was the last one. The last one was really terrible. I have a feeling that Dusko Tadic at that moment had stepped backward. I do not know whether the barrel was out of my mouth at that moment or before that, but I received a terrible blow there and everything burst. I fell. I fainted. I do not know for how long I was down.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: While you were standing there with the barrel of the gun in your mouth, you said you were being hit on the head with double blows. Who was hitting you at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A person I did not know, because I could not -- I had no opportunity of taking a glance at that other person. I do not know who it was.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: In addition to this person that you did not know, was anyone else hitting you with a baton?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dusko Tadic was hitting me with a metal spring and that other person with a rubber baton, and it was really ugly. I was receiving those blows while this barrel is in my mouth, and my head was swinging left and right. A double blow is the worst one and they were hitting me together.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: How was Dusko Tadic able to hit you with this metal object if he had the barrel in your mouth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was holding this machine gun on his left shoulder.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: He was hitting you with his other hand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With his right hand.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: You indicated that after this last very hard blow to the back of your head, you fell. Did you become unconscious for a time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What happened after you regained consciousness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I regained consciousness, what I saw, I saw where I was. I did recover somewhat. I had fallen and then at that point somebody in the boots was there, in soldier's boots was there. I cannot forget ever that thing. I am just recovering, I am regaining consciousness and I see the soldier's boots and I am on the floor, I am on the ground. Then the order came not far from me, perhaps a metre, a metre and a half away, there was a body and that was awful. The man was lying down. He did have a head and did not have a head because the head had been crushed. You could not identify a nose or eyes or any part of his body only blood, blood, blood.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then Dusko Tadic told me to hit the man lying down on the head.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Regrettably, I had to.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: When you hit the man what was the sensation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Unspeakable. When we used to train, to coach, and you have your sparring partner, you do not hit that man directly. You can only reach as far as this body. I did not want to hit that man, but unless I hit him I had no choice. I hit the man and then something came out of his head. I did not hit him much. I cannot say what, but a scream, no, it was not a scream, it was something, something which one really cannot experience in normal conditions. Something came out of that head, a sound. I do not know what it was.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What happened after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that from a room two civilians unknown to me came out and they were carrying a camera, and they walked towards us and Dusko Tadic said then, told me to flee downstairs, to get away downstairs. I could barely stand up and, as I was going down the stairs, then there is a sort of a semi-turn to the right and I hitted down there and I ricocheted from that wall. It was horrible, but I managed to return to people, to my group, by myself.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: At this time I would like to ask that this photograph along with a black and white copy be marked as Prosecution Exhibit 250A and B for identification. After that is marked, if that could be shown to the Defence and then provided to the witness? Sir, do you recognise what is depicted on that photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise it very well.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Does that photograph depict the area near the top of the stairs on the first floor of the administration building at the Omarska concentration camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, for clarification 250A would be the colour photo and B would be the black and white copy. (To the witness): Sir, at this time if you could put the black and white copy on the overhead projector?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: If we could zoom back, please, so that we can see that? Thank you. That is good right there. If you would take one of the red pens that are on the table there? There are two red pens. If you could take one of those, please, and if you could first point for us to the area where you were standing when this incident began?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The person I did not know was standing here and I was next to him.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Could you please take that red pen and, if you would, please, where you were standing put the letter "W" -- if you could press hard to be sure that that can be seen -- and where the younger detainee was standing, if you could use that pen and put "W1"? Sir, if you could point to the position where Dule Tadic was standing and if you could take that red pen and put the letter "T" in that position?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, "T".

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (The witness indicated on the photograph).

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: You mentioned that at some point you saw a man, Rade Knezevic, standing and watching what was going on. Could you point to where Rade Knezevic was when you saw him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: So he was standing by the door that is depicted on the right side of the photograph as you look at it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, here at that door.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, at this time I would tender Prosecution Exhibit 250A and B for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: There is no objection, your Honour. Perhaps the Prosecution would be good enough to provide us with a copy?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Exhibits 250A and 250B will be admitted and you will provide the Defence with a copy, please, immediately.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. (To the witness): Mr. Mrkalj, during this incident you have just described in total how long did you actually see Dule Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I had enough time to be able to identify him. At the moment when my head was straightened I could see, he was, well, roughly about this and then there is the length of the baton, so he was in my immediate vicinity, eye to eye.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Sir, if you can estimate during this incident the total time that you saw Dule Tadic -- was it seconds, was it minutes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Several minutes, I think, I could not be more precise, but several minutes -- enough never to forget him, enough.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Do you recall what Dusko Tadic was wearing during this incident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was wearing blue police jacket, buttoned up. He was also wearing soldier's boots.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Do you recall anything about those boots?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was blood on those boots, fresh blood.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Could you describe his physical appearance at the time you saw him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, he looked, well, a rounded face. He had a beard, not a normal beard. He was unshaven. At the first glance he looked as if perspiring, as if he had been doing something. There was sweat. I could see his cynicism. I could see his grin in his look, as if he was enjoying himself.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: You indicated that he had a beard, not a normal beard, he was unshaven. Could you describe for us, please, this beard? Was it a long full beard? Did it appear to be some days growth? Could you describe that for us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I do not know whether his facial hair grows quickly or not, but he was unshaven, for how long I do not know, 10 days, I do not know. It is really difficult to determine. It varies from one man to another. It depends really on how quickly his facial hair grows. He had a growth.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: During that incident did you ever hit or attempt to hit any of the men who were beating you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What physical injuries did you suffer as a result of the beating you received?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that people said I would not survive. I had even said goodbye to some people. I could not walk without having somebody holding my head for several days. It was terrible, especially when there would be more than 600 of us in the restaurant, then everybody had to stand up and I could not. There was no room. I can never forget the help that people gave me who were so thoughtful, who took me, Agan Sekiric, then Mulalic. My teeth were in a very bad shape. They had been knocked together. I had no care. It was very hard. In Manjaca, a tooth was pulled out. I think that doctor's name was Leopold we called him "Dr. Leo". It was pulled out in a very primitive way. It was very hard. The effects were somewhat -- showed up later. I underwent three surgeries. The first surgery I underwent as soon as I arrived in Karlovac, I was in a very -- I was in an awful shape.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Mr. Mrkalj, were all three of these surgeries on your gums and mouth to correct the injuries you had received?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: You had indicated that you received blows to your right hand. Did you suffer any damage to that hand as a result of those blows?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: How long did you suffer the effect of those blows on your hand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About three, for the past three months I have been able to use it normally, to do everything with it; until then I could not put it like that. It was painful, terrible pain. Now it is much better, much better.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: After this beating that was given to you by Dusko Tadic, do you recall an occasion when visitors came to the concentration camp and prisoners were lined up and ordered to sing Serbian songs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Were these visitors accompanied by any Serb leaders that you recognised?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Who was that that you recognised?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I recognised Simo Drljaca, Simo Miskovic, Dule Jankovic and Vojo Kupresanin who must have come from Banja Luka. He is a politician.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Were any of the camp leaders there to greet these visitors?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Zeljko Meakic was the Commander at the time and there were also the shift heads.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you notice anything about the license plates of the cars that those visitors were brought to the camp in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. One of the vehicles had the license plates beginning with number, with the figure "9" and another one with "6".

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: You had indicated earlier that "9" had a significance to you and that had indicated the federal SUP. What did the number "6", what significance did that have to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "6" means, "6" indicates the territory of the Republic of Serbia, that is, that vehicle should be owned by someone in the Republic of Serbia, since police vehicles had, the police vehicles in the Republic of Serbia had "6" as the first number on their plates, Bosnia-Herzegovina had No. 1. I mean, each Republic had a different number.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: When you left Omarska where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was taken to Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Who arranged the transport of the detainees to Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The transport Commander was Milan Gavrilovic.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: How were you transported to Manjaca, what type of vehicles?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were taken by buses of Auto Service Ljubija and Auto Transport Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Where did you go from there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We went to Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: After Manjaca where did you go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After Manjaca, when Manjaca was closed down, I came to the Republic of Croatia. It was organised through UNHCR.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Mr. Mrkalj, would you please look around the courtroom and tell us if you see Dusko Tadic in the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I will. That is this garbage over there.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Sir, if you would refrain from such comments, please?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Please do. Just identify, if you can, the accused.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Would you please tell us where he is sitting in the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He is sitting there in front of me between two policemen.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would ask that a proper identification be noted.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes. The record will reflect that the witness has identified the accused.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Mr. Mrkalj, prior to the attacks in opstina Prijedor in May 1992, were you a member of any anti-Serb military or paramilitary organisation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Were you a member of any organised anti-Serb resistance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: After the beginning of these attacks were you a member of any such organisation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, regrettably not.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Sir, as a result of the attacks and other events in the opstina of Prijedor, have you lost any family members who are either dead or missing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we lost 52 members.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: No further questions, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Mrkalj, the first matter I want to ask you about is whether you have discussed the evidence that you were going to give today with any other witness in this case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Or whether you have been told about the evidence of any other witness in this case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Or whether you have been watching through television or reading reports about the evidence being given in this case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What I am interested in then is the matter of the flower pots on the pista that were pointed out to you in a photograph earlier this morning. Do you recollect that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Perhaps if we could have on our screen then these particular containers as shown in, I believe it is, Exhibit 247?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: I believe that is 246.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: 246. If that could be put on the video monitor so that we can all see it? Thank you. Perhaps it can be adjusted so that we can take the light off the right-hand side which we have at the moment and perhaps any reflection be shown on the left-hand side? Thank you very much, Mr. Bos. (To the witness): You recollect being shown this photograph earlier today, Mr. Mrkalj?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What I am interested in is your opinion that there would have been greater spaces between these containers at the time that you were on the pista?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you recollect giving that opinion earlier today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We have available to us, just so that you know, photographs showing the whole of this area with those containers, and this is not the only photograph that shows them. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: These containers mark the boundary between the administration building and the large hangar building on both sides, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The spacing that we have within this photograph before the Court is what I suggest to you is the regular and ordinary spacing of the containers on the pista? Do you disagree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I stick to my earlier statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Perhaps if you could repeat that so that I am sure as to what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Why not. There was larger, bigger spacing, I am quite convinced of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So what you are saying is that extra containers have been put in position on the pista and the grouping of the containers put in such a way to give a less space ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is what you are saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: --- between the containers. I am trying to find out what you are saying and what the logic of what you are saying, whether it exists? I am sorry to have to ask you about this, but it is my job to test your evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just go ahead, ask your questions. I will reply to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You would be saying that there is a greater spacing between those containers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we have photographs of these containers showing regular spacing of them between the buildings, photographs that were taken after August 1992, it would seem that you would be saying that extra containers have been added, and that those containers have all been adjusted and moved to give a representation such as we see in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Has it been translated for you, Mr. Mrkalj? Did you hear the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Perhaps Mr. Bos can check with whether the right channel is on the desk. Perhaps someone could advise me whether the question I put was translated?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Why do you not repeat the question. He says he believes there is more space and you are suggesting the logic of it. Did someone add them or what?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. What I am asking you to consider, if there are photographs showing the regular spacing of these containers taken after August 1992 at the distance we see in this photograph, are you saying that containers were added and the grouping, spacing of the containers adjusted to give the representation in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I stick to the statement that I gave earlier. There was greater spacing between the containers during the time I was in the concentration camp in Omarska. As far as the photographs that were made later, I cannot say anything about them. I am just telling you about the state of affairs in the camp when I was there, what I witnessed with my own eyes, and I am telling you about that and nothing beyond that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You see, this photograph was in fact taken during August 1992 when this camp was operating, and it was material taken by a television news team who went to the camp on a day and met Mr. Drljaca, Nada Balaban, and they filmed this at the beginning of August 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am just repeating what I said earlier. There was greater spacing than the one shown in this photograph. What happened later I do not know, nor can I confirm because I did not see that. What I see now, there was greater spacing earlier and that is what I claim.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You are not prepared to consider that you could be mistaken or wrong about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am still of the same view, it was greater spacing and I stand behind my words.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Very well. I want now to turn to events that you have described as taking place on 16th June 1992. What I would like you to tell me is how you were aware of that particular date. Counsel for the Prosecution gave it to you and you agreed, but I want to know whether you know and how you know of that particular date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not take advice from anybody. Let me first reply to that question. I speak on my own behalf. I came here without advisers, without instructions, and I am talking about what I have personally seen and experienced. So, please ask a concrete question what you are interested in. I have no advisers, nor do I need any.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Mrkalj, this is cross-examination and Mr. Kay is testing your testimony. He is entitled to put these questions to you. It is your responsibility to respond to them, not to make any guess as to why he is asking or what is the reasoning. Respond to his questions. If you cannot respond to his questions, then say you do not understand the question and then he will attempt to rephrase it. Will you do that, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Please, it was translated to me that I was given advice from advisers and I answered that particular question.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will give a very concrete answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If I can put this again. You said a particular incident happened to you concerning Dusko Tadic on 16th June 1992. What I would like to know is how do you know that date? Where did that information come from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had a wristwatch on my person at the time showing dates. I could tell what the date was and that date was interesting, the most interesting day and the saddest day for me personally because I was beaten up, but I also connect this day with another fact. In the concentration camp of Omarska a list was made of all the people. We were registered on 16th June 1992, and when I was taken out of a group of 30 and taken upstairs in the administration building we were listed in the books. So I stick to my earlier statement that it was 16th June 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did that wristwatch remain with you during your confinement in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it did not. It was seized.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you have any particular reason to look at the date on your wristwatch on that particular day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is my part of my professional deformation, defect, to look at the watch. It was part of my service when I was on duty. My work was always connected with time limits and in every situation I had to look at my watch and write down the time and the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Perhaps you could then help me with what time it was that this incident took place in the administration building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, about 2 o'clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Is that in the afternoon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you went up to the administration building with this younger person, were you given the reason for your going there by a guard or someone else?
