utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were standing, as I said, in a line. One of the guards came up to us and pointed at me, and said, "You and you, come upstairs to carry a body out."

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you went into the building you had your head bowed, as you have told us, looking at the ground, which was the way that you had to move around the camp, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I had my head bowed. I did say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you got to the landing at the top of the stairs in the administration building, again that was how your head would have been positioned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we had to hold that position until the next order.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So, when you got to the landing at the top of the stairs, did you wait facing against the wall that we have seen in the photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we did not face the wall. The wall was behind our backs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So you were facing out into the landing, but your head was bowed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not face the landing. As I stood I was not facing the staircase because the staircase was on my left. We were practically in the corridor of the first floor of the administration building. Under normal conditions we would be facing the door which I pointed out where Rade Knezevic was standing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you arrived at the corridor at the top of the stairs, did you just stop to wait for the next order? Did you expect someone to then tell you at some stage to do something?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we expected something, but there was laughter, as I said previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It was then after that laughter that you experienced the young person next to you receiving a blow?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You could not tell who had delivered that blow because you were looking down to the ground?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that the blow was delivered by Dusko Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That is something that you think.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am certain of that. Not only do I think but I am certain of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You told us earlier this morning that you had not seen how many people were around this area where you were standing against the wall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was not able to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It was when a baton was put under your throat that your head was lifted for the first time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, my head was lifted. Then I was able to see in front of me face-to-face Dusko Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You say that you have known Dusko Tadic and met him several times over the course of the previous year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: He knew someone that you knew called Emir Karabasic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Who was a policeman?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was a policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And you were a policeman?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you said about the monthly meetings where you would get to a bar or cafe earlier than the meeting so that you could talk together, are you saying that Dusko Tadic was present in those circumstances?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not -- it is not -- I am saying that, but I have already said Dusko was present, Dusko Tadic was present, and I met him on such an occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So he would have known that you were a policeman?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: But the person in the corridor who lifted your head up with a baton apparently did not know what your job was, because you told us that he asked what your occupation was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a good question, because the question was asked for reasons of cynicism, his grin, his smile.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yet in this conversation with the man in the corridor you have not referred to him using your name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said what his name was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You have given his name in this courtroom, but from your evidence earlier today I do not think we heard ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not understand the earlier question, I am sorry. It was not translated to me that way.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: What earlier question? Mr. Kay had not finished a question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The earlier question when I was asked if I had said my name.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In the evidence that you gave earlier today you did not tell us that you had used your name or he had used your name when speaking to you in the corridor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We must go back to the earlier question. This was not translated to me that way. I did not say ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We are having a difficulty understanding each other. Mr. Kay is cross-examining you and what he is saying is that Mr. Tadic never used your name before. You have to just answer the question that he asks without, I would suggest, trying to understand why he is asking this. I think I understand why you are asking it and that seems to be the problem. The question is, had Mr. Tadic used your name before when he was referring to you. Had he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is -- no, my name was not mentioned.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So then he says to you, "What do you do?" then of course you have testified that the reason you feel that he said that was cynicism, but keep in mind this is cross-examination. Answer the questions if you understand them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would appreciate it if the translators would not take turns so frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I will go back a bit, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I think I understand your point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: But you may rephrase and re-ask, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I do not want to disorientate the witness from the question. (To the witness): During there incident in the corridor the man you say was Dusko Tadic did not use your name Edin Mrkalj?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he did not use my name.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you looked at that man, did you in fact think that he looked older than Dusko Tadic looked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not think so. It was Dusko Tadic and at that moment I recognised Dusko Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you had described him from earlier occasions, can you remember whether he had a beard or not before May 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On previous encounters in 1991 he did have a beard.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: By "a beard" we mean a proper long beard, is that right, not just being unshaven?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, a proper long beard.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The person you saw during this attack upon you in the corridor did not have the same kind of beard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, at that moment he did not. I have already said on different occasions I was with Dusko Tadic. We greeted each other. I was able to see him without a beard and with a beard. It is a specific feature. When we say "beard" we mean a proper beard. So I stick to my earlier statement that Dusko Tadic at that time did have a beard, not a big beard, but he had not been shaven for a period of 10 days. As I say, I cannot -- I do not have the information how fast his facial hair grows but he was unshaven.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did that person in the corridor look different from the man that you knew as Dusko Tadic from before the conflict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was Dusko Tadic and in those moments his appearance which you ask me about was not the same as previously, on our previous encounters. I already mentioned his cynicism. One could see a certain pleasure in his face for some reason that is not quite clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I am actually interested in appearance and description. I will ask you this again. Was the appearance of the person different, not their character but the way the person looked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it was Dusko Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Perhaps you would like to look at a statement that you have made in relation to these proceedings, and I will give it to you in your own language as well as have to hand the original in English. In view of the time, your Honour, it might be better if we put these matters together and deal with them after the short adjournment.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I was going to suggest perhaps you could move to another area and come back to the statements, but if you want to follow that that is acceptable. Yesterday Mr. Wladimiroff had offered for identification purposes a copy of a statement. I believe that he said that that was his only copy. He offered both the statement in the witness's language as well as the English translation. I merely want to say that if you wish you may withdraw your copy and have a copy made. In other words, the Registrar will either provide you with a copy or, if necessary, give you back the copy he gave and we will then substitute for our purposes a copy. The same with two these exhibits, if it is your your only copy we will be happy to see to it that you have a copy for your files.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I am much obliged, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We will stand in recess until 2.30. Over the lunch adjournment, Miss Hollis, talk with Mr. Mrkalj, please, and explain as you indicated that it is important for him to answer the questions. It is also very important, Mr. Mrkalj, that you avoid any invectives when you are referring to the accused in this case. You should refer to him as his name. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We will stand in recess until 2.30. (1.00 p.m.). (Luncheon Adjournment) (2.30 p.m.) PRIVATE

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If your Honour pleases? Mr. Mrkalj, I would like you to look at this statement which records an interview that took place with you between 27th and 29th April 1995. The first document that I hand to you -- your Honour, for purposes of tendering perhaps this could be marked D21 -- that is a record of that interview in your own language. The second document, Mr. Usher -- if this can be marked D21A -- is that interview taken in the form of the English translation. Do you recollect being interviewed in April of last year, Mr. Mrkalj?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: On that occasion you had an interpreter there who spoke to you in your own language and translated a statement that had been written in English to you, and you confirmed you understood what had been written, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If you look at the second document that was handed to you, you in fact see that your signature appears on the pages of that document, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Putting that to one side, if you look at the translation in your own language, I would like you to turn to page 4. The numbers are marked on the bottom right hand corner of each page. Can you see that? There is two paragraphs, the first one being the fourth paragraph from the bottom "Tesko", it begins, can you see that, and it refers to 183 centimetres. Can you see that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Perhaps you could read out that paragraph which starts "Tesko mi je ... " in your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "It is difficult for me to describe Tadic because he has changed since the time I saw him before. I remember that during the incident he looked about 40 years old, roughly my height, 183 centimetres, well built, dark hair, slightly curly with a beard".

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Perhaps you could read it more slowly and not at such a great pace because those listening in the courtroom have to hear how it is translated. If you could take that paragraph much more slowly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "It is difficult for me to describe Tadic".

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "He has changed since the time when I saw him before the conflict".

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "I remember that during the incident he looked about 40, about my height, 183 centimetres, well built".

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Dark hair, slightly curly, with a beard of some 10 to 15 days".

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If you could do the same in the next paragraph that begins with "Iz"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "For the time before the camp Tadic looked as between 28 and 35 years of age. When he beat me he looked, he appeared older to me".

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you remember before our break this morning that I asked you whether the man who attacked you looked different, whether the man you say was Dusko Tadic looked different in appearance from the man you said was Tadic before, do you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: All you could refer to was the fact of the cynicism that he had in his eyes, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did say I noticed cynicism in his eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In this statement that you made last year you said that the appearance of Tadic had changed since you saw him before the conflict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then in the statement I said, first, to clarify it, I signed it in English and, as regards his appearance and your question, I said that at the moment while I was being beaten his appearance changed, to my mind. I was referring to my psychological -- to the state of my mind, my mental state.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Just turn over the page to the very last page of that document in your own language on page 5?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You see there a certificate and you will see there a place where there is a space for a signature which you signed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Dated 29th April 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If you just care to look at what is written in that certificate in your own language as I read it out, "Witness acknowledgment. This statement has been read over to me in the Bosnian language and is true to the best of my knowledge and recollection. I have given this statement voluntarily and am aware that it may be used in legal proceedings before the International Criminal Tribunal for the Prosecution of persons responsible for Serious Violations of International Law committed in the territory of the former Yugoslavia since 1991, and that I may be called to give evidence in public before the Tribunal." You signed that acknowledgment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Also on the document is a certificate signed by the interpreter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Which gives a clear statement that this statement had been read back to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And you were informed of its contents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: As you have told us, you were a policeman?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I dare say that giving a statement for legal proceedings, as a policeman, you would take great care to ensure that what you had said was within that statement, would I be right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but in my -- I read it in my mother tongue, this statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, and it was read out to you in your mother tongue. The whole purpose of this is that there is an interpreter who does that for you, who has a duty and signs it. You are not saying that the interpreter has been making things up, are you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you repeat the question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You are not saying that someone has been making things up to put them in your statement, are you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that some changes occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Because it is difficult to see why someone from the Prosecution would want to insert in your statement as a Prosecution witness that the person they are accusing had changed in appearance, do you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When we look at that second paragraph you read out, "From before my time in the camp Tadic looked as he was between 28 to 35 years old. When he beat me in the camp, he looked older", and you have described him as being 40 years old. There seems to be a great difference in ages between the two men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I meant at that time, at that time when I knew him as a sportsman I gave that estimate. However, in the camp at Omarska, I mean this referred to the situation, to my very difficult mental condition. He looked, his shape, his face appeared older. He seemed to me tired. He looked sweaty. As for the height, I mean, to my mind he was at that time three metres tall, not one metre.83 because I was in a completely different mental state. That is what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So did the condition and your mental state, in fact, make it difficult for you to recognise and identify the man who was attacking you at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that is not what I mean. I am talking about the situation in which I was, that is, my mental state when I looked at him and I do remember the statement. When I looked at him from the floor upward, I mean, he looked terrible, older, completely different, but while I was still conscious and could look as I am looking at you now, face to face, then I could, I had enough time to recognise Dusko Tadic. So, this here refers to my bad mental condition, to those difficult moments.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Why did you not want to explain to us before we broke for lunch about those changes in the man who attacked you? Why did you not want to tell us about that? Why did I have to put this statement to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because you did not ask me about my mental state at that particular moment. If Dusko Tadic at that time appeared different, and if I remember well and I do remember well, you asked me at the very beginning whether I could see Dusko Tadic properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you, in fact, know Dusko Tadic at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Had you ever met him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Dusko Tadic was someone who lived in Kozarac. Did you live in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That is all I ask, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Miss Hollis, any redirect?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, thank you. Mr. Mrkalj, if you would refer again to the document that the Defence counsel referred to, that is the statement in your own language and if would you look at page 3 of that statement. If you would look, please, at the third paragraph beginning with the words, and I apologise for my pronunciation "U ovom incidentu Tadic", can you see which paragraph I am talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: If you would please look at the last sentence in that paragraph beginning with "Tadic", and if you would please read that statement, that sentence, for us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Tadic's face was dirty, hair was dirty, tired eyes as if from the lack of sleep and he was drunk".

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: When you saw Dusko Tadic that day in Omarska, is it this type of physical condition that you were talking about as being different?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you repeat the question, please? I did not get you quite well.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: When you saw Dusko Tadic that day in Omarska, is it this type of physical condition that you were talking about as being different?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Sir, the Defence counsel asked you if you were saying to the Court that the interpreter had been making things up in that statement. Are you saying that there was a mistake in the interpretation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think there was a mistake in interpretation, and it referred to a different kind of situation, that is not the state when I came, when I arrived, the first meeting. This referred when I was giving this statement, I was referring to when I was on the ground, I looked at him upward and that was the appearance.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: You understand that it is very important in proceedings such as these that you give the truth as you remember it, regardless of what that truth is, do you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: You have testified to these Judges in this courtroom that you recognised the man that day in Omarska as the Dusko Tadic who had been introduced to you by Emir Karabasic. Were you able, in fact, to recognise that man that day in Omarska as the Dusko Tadic who had been previously introduced to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that was Dusko Tadic and nobody else.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: You indicated during the cross-examination that you had previously seen Dusko Tadic prior to this incident in Omarska with a long beard. Can you tell the Court what you mean. When you had seen him before this incident in Omarska, had there been a long beard or a full beard? This is becoming somewhat confusing and if you could clarify that. Describe the beard he had before you saw him in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the longest beard he ever had was roughly like this.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: How many centimetres from his face?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, I would say about two or three, two to three centimetres.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: So you are talking about a full beard but not necessarily a long beard, would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not long.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: When you testified under direct examination, I believe you said that during this incident as the man with the baton raised your face so that you could see him, that when you saw him he asked you something to the effect, "How come you are here? What brought you here?" is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He asked me, yes, "How come that you came here?" and "What are you doing here?"

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: If you recall, what was the expression on his face at the time he asked you that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was very cynical. I felt cynicism in that question, as if it is, you know, a man knows why you are here and how you got there, but he tries to psychologically kill you and then he asks you a question of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: So it was after, is this correct, in your direct testimony I believe you indicated it was after he had asked you something to the effect, "How come you are here? What brought you here?" it was after that that Dusko Tadic asked you your profession, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: No further questions, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Just one other matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Mrkalj, when you say someone could be 28 years old, do you mean they are 40 years old?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am referring to a state, about knowing a man before and at the time of my very difficult mental condition, that is, when I was giving this statement, that is what he looked like, as a sportsman, that is. So I gave this approximate age, 28 to 35, up to 35. But in those very difficult moments, in that very painful condition that I was in, then I said he could have been 40.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Miss Hollis?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is one matter, perhaps, before the witness is excused. I am almost hesitant in the timing now, given some of the questions on cross-examination, but I would inform the Court that before we came back into session, a person from the interpretation section indicated to me, told me, that during the direct examination of this witness there had been a misinterpretation into English of what the witness had said. Dealing with the incident with Dule Tadic, there had been an English interpretation that Dule Tadic, Dusko Tadic, had a "submachine gun". The interpreter indicated to me that, in fact, what Mr. Mrkalj had said was that Dusko Tadic had an "automatic rifle". I would note that for the Court. If there is any question about that, we can have the interpretation section come in and explain that.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am sure it is a matter that can be checked according to the record of what was said and we will be advised as to what the actual translation was. It will not make my difference to my presentation of the cross-examination. I do not need to reopen any matter concerning that. I am sure we can deal with it after the session is finished today.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That is fine. My real question was, I suppose, whether you would have additional cross-examination in the light now of the understanding that it was an automatic rifle instead of a submachine gun.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK. We do not need to hear from the interpreter certainly before we release this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, I think it would be unnecessary.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK, very good. Anything else, Miss Hollis?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there any objection to Mr. Mrkalj being permanently excused?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Mrkalj, you are permanently excused. You are now free to leave. Thank you for coming today. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would call Hasiba Harambasic. HASIBA HARAMBASIC, called.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mrs. Harambasic, would you take the oath that is being given to you, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. (The witness was sworn)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Would you please state your name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Hasiba Harambasic.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What is your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 28th March 1942.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What is your nationality or ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am a Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What is your religion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Islamic, Islam.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was your place of birth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was born in Cazin.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What part of Bosnia is that located?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In western Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Was your maiden name Pozderac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Was that family name well known in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Why was it well known?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because they were statesmen.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was your prior occupation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was a dentist.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you practise dentistry in the town of Prijedor and also live in the town of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: How long did you live there and practise dentistry there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 29 years.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Where did you work in the town of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the medical centre called Dr. Mladin Stojanovic in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: You worked there until when?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Until I was put in the Omarska camp, 22nd June 1992.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What part of the town of Prijedor did you live in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The centre of town.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: The section of Prijedor that you lived in, what was the ethnic composition of that section?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mixed.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Was there any section of Prijedor that was predominantly Muslim?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Stari Grad, the old town.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you ever visit Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Why would you go there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, very often.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Why would you go there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had good friends there.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: As a result of your profession and also as a result of living in Prijedor for so many years, did you know many people from the Prijedor area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you know many of the community political and professional leaders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: To your knowledge, did Serb leaders in the town of Prijedor know of your family, the Pozderac family?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: In the elections that were held in Bosnia in the early 1990s what party won in the town of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The SDA, the Party of Democratic Action.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Were you in Prijedor when the Serbs took over control of the town on 30th April 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: After this Serb takeover in Prijedor, did you see an increase in the number of men in uniform in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: After the takeover was a work obligation levied on non-Serbs in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Who levied this work obligation on non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were announcements on the radio and TV, Banja Luka television studio. The order was that we must report to our work obligation.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: On whose authority were these announcements made?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the authority of the Crisis Staff of the city of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was this work obligation, what did it mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had to go to work. I would go there and I would sit in my surgery. I did not do any work.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Were you allowed to work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: After the Serb takeover in the town, did you notice an increase in the number of checkpoints in the town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What did you observe ---

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: -- and where did you observe these checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The checkpoints were in all institutions, at the health centre, in the bank, in the municipality building, in the streets, in the approaches to buildings -- all over the place.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you know any of the people who manned these checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: The people that you knew, what was their ethnic group or nationality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: These people who manned the checkpoints, what did they wear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They wore different uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What types of uniforms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were camouflage uniforms, JNA uniforms, black uniforms, camouflage uniforms with red berets, uniforms with black hats, with things hanging from the hat ---

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: I would like to direct your attention to ---

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- tassles.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: -- on about 30th May, on that date, did the inhabitants of Prijedor receive ultimatums?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We had to put out white flags on our balconies, on our fences, houses. In case we had to go out into the town, we had to put on white arm bands on our left arm.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: After that date, did you continue to live in your home until 22nd June?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: During that time, from about 30th May until 22nd June, did you see any sections of the city damaged or destroyed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the whole of Stari Grad was burned. The street across from my place. There were places of worship demolished, destroyed. Many houses had been destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: The street across from your place that was destroyed, to your knowledge, what was the ethnic group of the people who lived in those homes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: The places of worship that were demolished or destroyed, these were places of worship for what religion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Muslim places of worship.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Again during this same time period between about 30th May and 22nd June, was your home searched?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: How many times?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Four times.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you recognise any of the people who came to search your home?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did they tell you what they were searching for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were searching for weapons.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you have any weapons in your home?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What did they take from your home?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They took all gold objects, money and other valuables.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: These men who came to your home during these four visits, did you recognise the dialect of these men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Were all of these men speaking a local dialect?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What other dialect?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Serbian, from Serbia proper.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Were you able to lock your doors to keep these people out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because otherwise they would have shot at the door.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Beginning on 30th May, did you see people being taken away by Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you recognise any of the people being taken away?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, many of my friends were taken away.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was the ethnic group of these people you recognised?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Were any of these people you recognised in or had they been in positions of leadership in the community?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: I would like to draw your attention to 22nd June 1992. On that date were you arrested at your home?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Who arrested you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was arrested by three soldiers who came to my house in camouflage uniforms. One had remained behind on the staircase and two came into my dining room. They told me to get ready, not to take anything along, that I am just going for an interview to the SUP.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you recognise any of these men who came to arrest you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: How were you taken to the SUP for this interview?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was taken to the SUP in a police car, which had the popular name Black Maria.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: At the SUP were you interviewed or interrogated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was interrogated.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: How many times were you interrogated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Three or four times.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Who did the interrogation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mirjana Jankovic did the interrogation.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you know her?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only by sight.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you know what her position had been in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, she was a lawyer and a SUP inspector.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did she tell you why you were there being interviewed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: She had charges written in front of her. The first charge I was charged with that I was a friend of Zeljko Sikora who had found an injection for sterilizing Serbian women and baptising the children. The second charge was Dr. Dzafic in the prosthetic department, that I had been buying weapons in the Cazinska Krajina. The third was that Hakija Pozderac was leading the Green Berets in Cazin. The fourth one, that my daughter was a member of the Green Berets. The fifth one, that my son had not served in the Serbian Army. The sixth was that I had said that I would like to see all Serbs floating along the Sana River.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: This Zeljko Sikora, who was he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zeljko Sikora was a general practitioner. He was specialising in gynecology.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: The person you identified as Dr. Dzafic, what was his profession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dr. Dzafic was a specialist in prosthetic dentistry, in the dentistry department, my superior.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: These two men, what was their ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sikora was a Croat and Dr. Dzafic, Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Who was that Hakija Pozderac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Hakija Pozderac was my uncle. He used to be a statesman, the Minister of Foreign Affairs of the entire former Yugoslavia. He was in charge of the Olympic Games. He was the Secretary of the Association for Physical Culture of Yugoslavia, was also the President of the Association of Veterans of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Had you been involved with the dentist, Dr. Dzafic, in buying weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. I had -- I have never been involved.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: During these interrogations were you beaten?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was done to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was beaten badly. She pulled my hair. She slapped my face, and she hit me so badly that one of my teeth was knocked out.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you spend the night at the police station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Were any other detainees there with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Zlata Cikota was together with me.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you know her?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was her profession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: She was an engineer.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was her ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: While you were in the police station, did any Serb official visit you there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in the morning at 7.15 the following day, I was visited by my colleague, Srda Srdic. He used to be the President of the Serbian Democratic Party in Prijedor and told me that I was going to Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Were you and Zlata Cikota taken to Omarska from the SUP on 23rd June?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: How were you taken there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the same vehicle, the Black Maria.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Who took you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By Bato Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you know him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was his position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was a SUP policeman.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was his ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Serb.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: When you arrived at Omarska where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I arrived in Omarska I was taken to the central building.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Could you use the pointer, please, and show the Court, point to the building you call the central building? This is the smaller building to your right of the large, long, red building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Is this the building that had administrative offices and a restaurant?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: When you were taken to that building, were you asked questions there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I just gave personal information.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: When the people asking this personal information spoke to you, did they use your married name or your family name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Both, they used both names.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: How long were you held at Omarska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 42 days.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Do you recall about two days or three days after coming to the camp a man at the camp introducing himself to you as Zeljko Meakic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Had you known him from before the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you see him often at the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, every day and every night.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did he have a particular room that he used in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: In what building was that room located?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (The witness indicated on the model).

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: In this building you referred to as the central building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: The guards at the camp, what did they wear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All kinds of uniforms, camouflage uniforms. Half wore uniforms and half civilian clothes. They were dressed, all of them.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What type of weapons did they have, if you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Short automatic rifles and the big rifles.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you ever see a machine gun positioned while you were at the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, from our room a guard, from that place he could come to our room just by jumping over ---

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: So the machine ---

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- the fence.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: -- gun position was on the roof of the central building toward the front of the building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you know a Dr. Ivic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was my colleague.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was his position in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was the head of the Emergency Department in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did he ever come to Omarska camp while you were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, very often.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you know a man named Mico who was a medical technician or a nurse?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, well.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Would you describe this Mico?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Medium height, sturdily built, without one arm.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Mico and Dr. Ivic, what was their ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: During the times that you saw Mico and Dr. Ivic in Omarska camp, did you ever see them give any medical care to any of the detainees there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: While you were at Omarska, what building were you kept in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the central building.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: You do not need to point now. I will ask you to do some of that in a moment. During the night where were you kept?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was kept in the second room on the left-hand side upstairs.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: This would be on the first floor of this building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Where were you kept during the day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The whole time we were in the lunch room, in the dining room.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: About what time would you go upstairs at night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It depended on the guard, from 9.00, at 9.00, half past nine or 10.00 at the latest.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: When would you come down stairs in the morning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Between 5.00 and half past 5.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Were other women kept in the camp with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Do you recall roughly how many other women were kept in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 37 and a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Where were these other women kept?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were 19 women in our room and the remaining women were in the other room. Only one woman was never with us. Her name was Hajra Hadzic. She was in the white house all the time.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: You have indicated that one of the women there was a Serbian woman. What was the ethnic group of the other women, if you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were three Croats and the others were Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: While you were at Omarska, do you recall a woman there who was named Azra?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you see any injuries or wounds on Azra?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. She came to Omarska because she had been wounded. She came wounded.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What type of wounds did she have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: She said that she had been hit by a shell and that her wounds were from this hit by a shell.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Do you recall a woman in Omarska named Sadeta Medunjanin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do quite clearly. She was in my room.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Had she been kept in any other location prior to coming to your room?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, she was in the white house.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you see any injuries on her?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, she had a wound on her right hand and up to her elbows and above the knees. She had wounds from cigarettes being put out on her skin.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: To your knowledge, were other members of her family also at Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, her husband was there too, Beco Medunjanin, and her son, Anes Medunjanin.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: While you were in the camp, did you ever learn what happened to Beco Medunjanin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He disappeared.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Do you know what position Sadeta and her husband, Beco, had held in the Prijedor community?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Beco Medunjanin was in charge of the Secretariat of National Defence and his wife, Sadeta, was a teacher in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: While you were kept in the central building, did you ever see male detainees who were also kept in that building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Where were these detainees kept?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were kept in different places, in the building, in the glassed building, and in the evening those who had been on the pista would come to the dining room.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: You said they were kept in the "glassed building", what did you call that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What did you call that, that area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was an area which had a glass door so we women we called it a "glass house".

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: While you were at Omarska did you have to perform any duties in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What duties did you have to perform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What duties did you have to perform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We cleaned the place and washed. We did a lot of dish washing, about 3,100 pieces every day and for a time, for about 10 days, 10 or 15 days, I was in charge of distributing the food.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: You say that you cleaned, what areas did you clean, both ground floor and first floor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: I would like to ask you some questions about the work you did in the restaurant concerning the food. While you were at Omarska how often were the detainees there fed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One meal only.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What kind of food did they receive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Horrible, bad. They would be given -- first, we were given some vessels and there would be some water in it, some soup, with two or three cabbage leaves or, perhaps, one, two to three potatoes. If it was beans, it was very watery and it was usually rotten. Most of the food was already in a state of decay.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you ever see any of the detainees become ill immediately after eating the food?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, large numbers.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What amount of food would they receive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Half a bowl, half a ladle, perhaps less than half a plate.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: How was this food delivered to the restaurant building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was brought in a yellow TAM vehicle every day.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Do you happen to recall the number that was on the licence plate of that vehicle?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: I am sorry, you said 355-46?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: That is a pretty minor detail. How were you able to remember such a detail?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I kept remembering it.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For my own sake.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: At this time if Prosecution Exhibit 232, that is document Z327, could be brought up on the computer screen? Perhaps while that is being done, your Honour, we could move on? (To the witness): Do you know who the drivers were of this vehicle, this truck, that was used to deliver food?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What are the names, if you recall them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Pero Mrdja, Kobas, Mirko Dragan, Brane Drlic, but Pero Mrdja and Kobas usually drove the truck.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you know these people from before you were in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Was this truck used for any other purpose other than to deliver food?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it took away the dead.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: At this time, perhaps, the document could be called up on to the screen? Again that is Prosecution Exhibit 232, document 20-7. (To the witness): Can you look at this vehicle and tell us if you recognise this vehicle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do. That is the truck.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: That is the truck that you were describing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: When this food was delivered to the detainees, how long did they have to eat their meal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Three minutes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What would happen if they took longer than that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then they had to spill it away.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did all of the people get something to eat each day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, very often there was not enough food. So that sometimes more than half of the detainees would go on without food.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you ever see any of the detainees beaten as they came in to eat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, every day.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: The people that you saw come through the line to get their meals, did you notice any injuries or bruises or wounds on these people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What did you observe about their physical condition?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They looked terrible, emaciated, thin, dirty, with lice, beaten up, and they had open wounds all over their bodies, arms broken. A specific thing was that whenever I looked at people, they would have enormous bruises around their eyes, so-called natural eye glasses.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Was there any significance to these enormous bruises around their eyes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they came from blows into the head.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: You indicated that you had to clean rooms in the restaurant building, the central building. Would you find anything ---

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: -- unusual in those rooms when you cleaned them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we came across all sorts of objects. We found -- we would come across blood, bits of teeth, then huge metal rods or cables and then we would find there pieces of skin, all sorts of objects, urine. You could find everything in those rooms.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: These rooms where you found such things, where were these rooms located, on the ground floor, the first floor or both?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, those rooms were on the first floor.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: At this time, your Honour, if I could ask the technician to set up the camera very quickly? I would like the witness to point out some locations in this central building.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes. Can you do that quickly?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Ma'am, if you could take off those headphones after I tell you what to do -- put them back on for a moment -- after I tell you what I would like you to do, I will ask you to take those off. I would like you to come around to the front side of the model. You will see headphones with the extension wire. I would ask you to put those headphones on as soon as we have the camera set up here. Judge Stephen, I apologise for any obstruction here. We will not be long. If we could have the roof taken off the restaurant building for the first floor as well as for the restaurant area? Thank you. Ma'am, if you could please come around, put on these headphones and I am going to ask you to point to certain rooms. You will see there are numbers in those rooms, so after you point to the room, if you could tell us the number? If you could now come around and put these other headphones on? Ma'am, if you could first point out for us the room in which you slept? If you could first point out for us the room in which you slept?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Could you put the pointer in there again? Is there any way with that camera we can get closer in on that? Thank you. If you could point out the room that other women slept in?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: If you could, please, point out the rooms in which you would find the blood and teeth and other objects?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was B9, B10, B11, B3.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Was there a room there that Zeljko Meakic used?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was this large room, B1, it had a door here, and by the wall, some 10 centimetres from there, there was something with bed linen -- [We can barely hear the witness, I am sorry].

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: When I ask you the question you are going to have to speak into the microphone behind you. Would you please point again to the area where the machine gun position was? Could you point to the room through which the person gained access to that position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was room B12.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Could you point to that, please? Were there any bathrooms up on that floor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. There were two bathrooms. The first one was for the police, B7, and the other one was ours, B6.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Was there any room up there that was used by the shift commanders or the guards?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, across our room, the room No. 5, B5.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: In the hallway was there any position that there was normally a table and a chair or chairs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in the corner here in the corridor there was a table with three chairs and another one in another corner.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us where that was positioned in relation to the stairway?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As you enter, to the left from the staircase.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Can you show us the area that you worked in during the day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here in the dining room.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: When you would wash dishes, what area were you in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here, yes, also here, in the same room here in the corner.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: So this is a small area that is partially set off toward the back of the restaurant area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: That is in A22?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: You mentioned that there were some men kept in the restaurant building that were kept in what you called the glass house. Could you show us where that is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, A14.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Was there a building in the camp that you referred to as the red house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was this.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: You are pointing to the small red building that is across from the far end of the long red hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: It is down from the white house.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I am sorry, I cannot hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: That was down from the white house, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ma'am, if you could resume your seat? We will not need that camera. Ma'am, while you were in Omarska, you said there was a truck that was used to take away bodies. How often did you see corpses while you were in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Every day.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Was there ever an occasion that you saw a larger truck used to carry away dead bodies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, towards the end of July.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What did you see on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I was coming down the stairs, there was a huge glass and I saw a big truck called dump truck full of corpses. When the guards realised that we were looking in that direction, he turned us back to our rooms.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: So you were coming down these steps that are shown on the rounded portion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Down these stairs, yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: You were able to look through that glass to see the truck?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, a window, a glass window.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: On the night before you saw this, had you heard any unusual noises or seen anything unusual at the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, throughout the night we heard screams, moans, shots, so that nobody slept at night.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Were you later that next day after you had seen this large truck eventually taken down into the restaurant area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you see any unusual activity at the white house that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in front of the white house there was -- they were washing the whole white house with a hose.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: At this time I would ask that document No. Z3-20-17 be called up and ask that that be marked as Prosecution Exhibit next in line which will be 251 for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. MISS HOLLIS (To the witness): Ma'am, looking at this picture, you see a large yellow truck there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A yellow one, yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Do you recognise that type of truck?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Is that the type of truck that had the bodies in it on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: At this time I would offer Prosecution Exhibit 251 for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Exhibit 251 will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: We do have a hard copy, if the Court wishes that the photo itself be put into evidence. All right, your Honour. Thank you. Ma'am, to your knowledge ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We will leave this in evidence. It is marked as 251, but if you have an extra copy, sometimes you have given us an extra copy, so if you have an extra copy for our use, that would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, we do.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Ma'am, without naming any of the women, while you were in Omarska were women taken from your room at night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: How often were women taken out of your room?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Almost every night.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Who took them out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Guards.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Do you recall the names of any of the guards who took them out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Krkan Mladjo, Krkan, Lugar, Nedeljko, Zeljko Meakic.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Again, without naming the names of the women, did any of these women ever tell you what happened to them when they were taken out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were raped.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: While you were in Omarska do you recall the night when Sadeta Medunjanin and a woman named Edna Dautovic were taken from the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did either of those women sleep in the same room with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Sadeta Medunjanin did.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: You have indicated earlier that you knew Sadeta Medunjanin prior to coming to the camp.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you also know Edna Dautovic prior coming to the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I knew Edna Dautovic well. She was my son's colleague. They together attended the electrical technical school and they together matriculated.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: To your knowledge, what was her ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Do you recall what her age was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Edna was 21 years of age and Sadeta, 46.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: On this night that these two women were taken from the camp, what do you recall happening?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were called out the previous day. That evening a bus came on to the -- into the camp grounds. It was a blue bus, and it had in white letters "Una Trans Bihac Bosanska Krupa". On a part of the bus in black letters it said "Seselj".

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: How were you able to see this bus?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Through the window of the bathroom in the WC.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Which bathroom are you talking about? The one that the guards used?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Our bathroom. No, our bathroom where we took our baths and washed ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you actually see those women as they went to that bus?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you see any camp personnel there at the bus?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, almost all the guards and the list was read out by Drago Prcac and Zeljko Meakic was standing by.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: In addition to these two women, were any other detainees put on that bus?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I knew Adem and I knew Samir Resic.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: These two men that you knew, what was their ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Was there anything said about why these people were being put on this bus?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were to be exchanged in Bihac.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: After the night that you saw these two women being put on that bus, have you seen them or heard from them since that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Since you left Bosnia, have you been in contact with the families of these two women?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: To your knowledge, have the families of these two women ever heard from or been reunited with these women?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: If I could have at this time this document marked as the Prosecution Exhibit next in order which will be Prosecution Exhibit 252 for identification? If you would please show that to the Defence and then to the witness? If the elmo has been set up again, could that first be given to the witness? (To the witness): Ma'am, do you recognise the woman in that picture?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is Edna Dautovic.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Could we put that photograph on the overhead, please? For the Court, could you point to Edna Dautovic, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (The witness indicated on the photograph).

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it on video?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: It is on mine. It is fine.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, ma'am. If you would be seated, please? I would tender Prosecution Exhibit 252.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No objection, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: 252 will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
